## Notes on Jeremiah 32:23–44

**Structure (vv. 26–44)**
- Barnes splits God's answer in two. In vv. 26–35, Judah's sins are the cause of her punishment. In vv. 36–44, that punishment is meant to correct Judah, not destroy her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-27.htm
- Utley says chapters 30–33 are usually called "the Book of Consolation." Chapters 30–31 describe the new covenant, and chapters 32–33 the symbolic act that assures the people of a future. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-32

**v. 23**
- Constable: Israel took the land but didn't obey the Lord, either in the prophets' spoken messages or in the written Torah. That is why these disasters came. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-32.html
- Enduring Word: Israel received God's special favour, yet rebelled and disobeyed, and this was the reason for the coming disaster. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah grieves over the people's rebellions and the judgments they brought. He doesn't complain about what God has done or tell God what to do. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_032.cfm

**v. 24**
- Utley: In the ancient Near East, armies took walled cities by surrounding them and cutting off food. They piled earth mounds against the walls, and these held wooden frames carrying battering rams. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-32
- Constable: The siege was the peak of the disaster and fulfilled God's warnings. God was fully aware of what was happening. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-32.html
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah takes comfort that God sees the situation and knows how to fix it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_032.cfm

**v. 25**
- Precept Austin: The word "though" isn't in the Hebrew, but it captures the reproach in Jeremiah's voice. Jeremiah didn't understand what God was doing, so his prayer ends with a question. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Enduring Word: Jeremiah struggled to see why he should buy the field. The Chaldeans were sure to win, and even if God could restore the people, they didn't deserve it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Bridgeway: With the siege engines at the walls, Jeremiah wondered whether he had understood God's will correctly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-27.html

**v. 26–27**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): God hands Jeremiah's own words from v. 17 back to him. If nothing is too hard for God, restoring the land will not be hard either. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-27.htm
- Constable: By turning Jeremiah's statement into a question, God is asking whether Jeremiah really believes it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-27.html
- Poole: "Flesh" stresses how weak humans are; no one can block God's plans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-27.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: The title comes from Numbers 16:22 and 27:16 and means the God on whom every person's life and death depends. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-27.htm
- Gill notes other ancient readings of the question: the Targum and Syriac have "Is anything hidden from me?", and another reading is "too wonderful for me?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-27.htm
- GotQuestions: "All flesh" is a common biblical phrase for all living people, here pictured as powerless and perishing. The question is rhetorical, since Jeremiah had already said it in v. 17. https://www.gotquestions.org/God-of-all-flesh.html
- Spurgeon: The question is the strongest possible way of saying nothing is too hard for God. Even a believer who already acted on this truth, as Jeremiah did when he bought the field, needs God to make it real to him personally. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/is-anything-too-hard-for-the-lord
- Calvin: Jeremiah faced what looked like a contradiction and had to throw his worry onto God. God comforts him by saying nothing is difficult for Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-27.html

**v. 28**
- Keil & Delitzsch: God repeats that Jerusalem will be given to Nebuchadnezzar and burned, because of Israel's long idolatry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-27.htm

**v. 29**
- JFB: The people worshipped a god of fire, so fire will be the means of their punishment. "To provoke me" shows they did it on purpose, not just that it turned out that way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/jfb/jer/jer_032.cfm

**v. 30–31**
- A note on the studylight page (I couldn't tell who wrote it): God's great acts for Israel began in Egypt, and so did Israel's sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-31.html
- Keil & Delitzsch on v. 31: The city became "a burden on my wrath," something that called God's anger out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-27.htm
- Utley calls v. 31 "a strange verse." He thinks it's an exaggeration for effect, showing how God reacts to idolatry. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-32

**v. 32**
- Utley: Everyone, from king to peasant, was unfaithful, including the priests and prophets who should have known better. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-32
- Precept Austin: The "therefore" in v. 36 draws its conclusion from this list of sins in vv. 29–35. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary

**v. 34**
- Smith: They set up abominations inside the temple itself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-34.html

**v. 35**
- Barnes: This repeats 7:30–31 with two changes: "Baal" replaces "Tophet," and "to Molech" replaces "in the fire." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-35.html
- Gill: This Baal is probably the same as Molech ("lord" and "king"). The words "through the fire" aren't in the Hebrew but are rightly supplied from other passages. Some think the children were only held over the flame or passed between fires as a purification, not burned to death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-35.htm
- Calvin also calls it a kind of purification rite, and says "Baal" covers every kind of idol. The editor's footnote on his page disagrees, pointing to 7:31 and 19:5, which say the children were burned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-35.html
- Geneva Bible note: The "high places" were altars for sacrificing to idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-35.htm

**v. 36**
- JFB reads it as "But now, nevertheless." Their guilt deserved lasting punishment, but God will restore them anyway, for the sake of His chosen people and His covenant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/jfb/jer/jer_032.cfm
- Calvin: The people couldn't be restored until they had first gone into exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/jeremiah/32.htm

**v. 37**
- Precept Austin says "all the lands," not just Babylon. The ten northern tribes never came back from Assyria, and the return didn't bring lasting safety. So the promise must point to a future fulfilment. It cites Jerome (via the Treasury of Scripture Knowledge) saying it wasn't fully kept for those who returned. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary

**v. 38**
- Ellicott: This is the old covenant formula from Exodus 6:7 and Deuteronomy 14:2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-39.htm
- Henry: God commits everything He is and has to their good. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-39.html

**v. 39**
- Keil & Delitzsch: God renews them through His Spirit, so they fear Him with one mind and stop wandering down many wrong paths. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-39.htm
- Calvin: The prophet is speaking of regeneration (new birth). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-39.html
- Henry: God promises to produce in them the fear He asks of them. Teachers can put things into our heads, but only God can put them into our hearts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-39.html
- Poole: "One heart" means agreement in true worship rather than a split between idolatry and true worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-39.htm
- Clarke: There is one object of worship and one way of salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-39.html
- Barnes: It means walking the one narrow path (Matthew 7:14), and "for ever" means every day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-39.htm
- Cambridge Bible: The wording echoes Deuteronomy 4:10 and 6:24. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-39.htm

**v. 40**
- Precept Austin and Constable: This is the new covenant of 31:31–34. Constable adds that "everlasting" isn't said in the chapter 31 passage. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-40.html
- Barnes: God promises not to turn away, and He also plants His fear in them so they don't depart. Together these make the covenant certain to last. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-40.htm

**v. 41**
- Barnes: "Assuredly" means "in truth" and refers to God's firm purpose, not the people's safety. God's rejoicing shows this is a covenant of grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-38.html
- Pulpit Commentary: Literally "with faithfulness," meaning complete sincerity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-41.htm
- Calvin: God takes on human feelings so that we can understand Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-41.html
- Clarke: Nothing pleases God more than our coming to Him to receive the good He longs to give. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-41.html
- Gill: God rejoices over them as a bridegroom over his bride. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-41.htm

**v. 42**
- Utley: The Old Testament sees God as the one source of everything and recognises no secondary causes. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21206
- Keil & Delitzsch: Deliverance will come as surely as the disaster did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-39.htm

**v. 43–44**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Listing the regions makes the promise stronger. Benjamin is named because Jeremiah's field at Anathoth was there. They also explain the Hebrew behind "restore them." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-39.htm
- I left out Enduring Word's v. 44 note because the page labels that paragraph AI-generated.

## Where traditions differ

**v. 40: can God's people fall away?**
- Calvin quotes Augustine's phrase for it, "indefectible constancy," and says it is far greater than what Adam had. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-40.html
- JFB: Both conversion and perseverance (staying faithful to the end) are God's work alone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-40.htm
- Gill: Believers may sin and partly drift, but they won't finally and fully turn away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-40.html
- Spurgeon preached v. 40 as a sermon on the everlasting covenant of grace, which gives believers "eternal security." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/jeremiah-32.html
- Benson, a Methodist, also says the Spirit produces perseverance. He applies the promise to Jews who embrace the gospel, and to the nation once it is converted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-40.htm
- Studylight labels Clarke "Arminian… Wesleyan/Methodist." His v. 41 note stresses people coming to receive God's good. That is a different emphasis, but he doesn't directly deny eternal security in what I read.
- I couldn't get Wesley's own note on 32:40.

**vv. 37–41: who is the promise for?**
- Precept Austin: A future gathering of Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Poole: Jews who receive Christ, or else a national conversion not yet fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-40.htm
- Gill: The gospel church first planted in Judea, plus a future settling of the converted Jews in their land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-41.htm
- Henry: Getting the land back is a picture of far greater spiritual blessings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_032.cfm

**Other views:** Jerome's note in the v. 37 entry is the only one I found, and it was quoted secondhand.
